track.name: Advanced Python
track.description: The features that separate scripting from real Python engineering — comprehensions, decorators, generators, OOP, typing, and the patterns pros actually use.

cards.title: List comprehensions
cards.explanation: A list comprehension builds a list in one line: `[x*2 for x in nums if x > 0]`. It's faster than a manual for-loop with `.append()` and reads more like the intent — 'doubled positives' instead of 'create list, loop, check, append'.
cards.takeaway: Comprehensions: build lists by intent, not by steps.

cards.title: Dict and set comprehensions
cards.explanation: The same syntax works for dicts (`{k: v for ...}`) and sets (`{x for ...}`). Great for inverting a dict, deduplicating while transforming, or building lookup tables in a single expression.
cards.takeaway: Comprehensions work for dicts and sets too.

cards.title: Unpacking and starred expressions
cards.explanation: Python lets you unpack iterables into variables: `a, b, *rest = [1, 2, 3, 4]`. The same `*` and `**` work for merging lists and dicts, spreading args into functions, and pulling apart return values cleanly.
cards.takeaway: `*` and `**` unpack and spread almost anything.

cards.title: *args and **kwargs
cards.explanation: `*args` collects extra positional arguments into a tuple; `**kwargs` collects extra keyword arguments into a dict. They let a function accept any number of inputs — useful for wrappers, decorators, and flexible APIs.
cards.takeaway: *args = extra positionals; **kwargs = extra keywords.

cards.title: Lambdas: tiny inline functions
cards.explanation: A lambda is a one-line anonymous function: `lambda x: x * 2`. They shine when passed to `sorted`, `map`, or `filter` — but if you'd need a docstring or more than one expression, write a real `def` instead.
cards.takeaway: Lambdas for one-liners; def for everything else.

cards.title: Closures
cards.explanation: When a function defined inside another function remembers variables from the outer scope, that's a closure. It's how you build function factories — like a `make_multiplier(n)` that returns a function which always multiplies by `n`.
cards.takeaway: Inner functions remember their outer scope.

cards.title: What is a decorator?
cards.explanation: A decorator is a function that wraps another function to add behavior — logging, timing, caching, auth checks — without touching the original code. You apply one with `@decorator_name` right above a function definition.
cards.takeaway: Decorators add behavior without editing the function.

cards.title: Writing your own decorator
cards.explanation: A decorator is just a function that takes a function and returns a new one — usually wrapping it with extra logic via `*args, **kwargs`. Use `functools.wraps` so the wrapped function keeps its original name and docstring.
cards.takeaway: Wrap, return, and use functools.wraps.

cards.title: yield and lazy iteration
cards.explanation: A function with `yield` becomes a generator — it produces values one at a time and pauses between them, instead of building the whole list in memory. Perfect for streaming files, infinite sequences, or anything large.
cards.takeaway: yield = produce values lazily, one at a time.

cards.title: Generator expressions
cards.explanation: Swap the `[]` of a list comprehension for `()` and you get a generator expression — same syntax, but it produces items on demand. Use it inside `sum()`, `any()`, or `max()` to avoid building a throwaway list.
cards.takeaway: () instead of [] = lazy version of a comprehension.

cards.title: Classes and __init__
cards.explanation: A class is a blueprint for objects; `__init__` is the constructor that runs when you create one. `self` refers to the instance — it's how methods access and modify the object's own data.
cards.takeaway: Class = blueprint; __init__ = setup; self = this instance.

cards.title: Inheritance
cards.explanation: A subclass inherits attributes and methods from a parent class and can override or extend them. Use `super().__init__(...)` to call the parent's setup so you don't duplicate logic.
cards.takeaway: Subclasses extend parents — call super() to reuse.

cards.title: Dunder methods
cards.explanation: Methods like `__str__`, `__repr__`, `__len__`, `__eq__`, and `__add__` let your objects work with Python's built-in operators and functions. Implement them and your class can be printed, compared, added, or measured naturally.
cards.takeaway: Dunders make your class feel native.

cards.title: @classmethod vs @staticmethod
cards.explanation: A `@classmethod` takes the class as its first arg (`cls`) and is great for alternative constructors. A `@staticmethod` takes neither `self` nor `cls` — it's just a function living inside the class for organization.
cards.takeaway: classmethod knows the class; staticmethod knows nothing.

cards.title: Dataclasses
cards.explanation: Decorate a class with `@dataclass` and Python auto-generates `__init__`, `__repr__`, and `__eq__` from the type-annotated fields. It's the cleanest way to write data-holding classes without 20 lines of boilerplate.
cards.takeaway: @dataclass = free __init__ and __repr__.

cards.title: try / except / finally
cards.explanation: Wrap risky code in `try`, catch specific errors with `except SomeError`, and use `finally` for cleanup that must always run. Catching bare `except:` hides bugs — always name the exception you actually expect.
cards.takeaway: Catch specific errors; use finally for cleanup.

cards.title: Custom exceptions
cards.explanation: Subclass `Exception` to define your own error types like `PaymentFailedError`. Custom exceptions make error handling readable — callers can catch exactly what they care about instead of parsing error messages.
cards.takeaway: Custom exceptions let callers catch by meaning.

cards.title: The with statement
cards.explanation: `with open(...) as f:` automatically closes the file when the block ends — even if an error happens. Any object with `__enter__` and `__exit__` works the same way: open a resource, use it, guarantee cleanup.
cards.takeaway: with = guaranteed setup and cleanup.

cards.title: Build one with @contextmanager
cards.explanation: The `contextlib.contextmanager` decorator turns a generator into a context manager — code before `yield` is setup, code after is cleanup. Way less ceremony than writing a class with `__enter__` and `__exit__`.
cards.takeaway: @contextmanager: setup, yield, cleanup.

cards.title: Type hints basics
cards.explanation: Annotate variables and function signatures with types: `def greet(name: str) -> str:`. Python doesn't enforce them at runtime, but tools like mypy and your IDE use them to catch bugs before you run the code.
cards.takeaway: Type hints catch bugs at edit time, not runtime.

cards.title: Optional, Union, and generics
cards.explanation: Use `list[int]`, `dict[str, User]`, `X | None` (or `Optional[X]`), and `X | Y` (or `Union`) to describe richer types. They make APIs self-documenting — the signature alone tells you what's allowed.
cards.takeaway: Richer hints = signatures that explain themselves.

cards.title: enumerate and zip
cards.explanation: `enumerate(items)` gives you `(index, item)` pairs; `zip(a, b)` walks two iterables in parallel. Together they replace 90% of the manual index-juggling you might be tempted to write.
cards.takeaway: Reach for enumerate/zip before tracking indexes by hand.

cards.title: itertools essentials
cards.explanation: The `itertools` module gives you `chain`, `groupby`, `combinations`, `product`, `accumulate`, and more — all lazy and memory-efficient. Anytime you're nesting loops to combine or group things, check itertools first.
cards.takeaway: Nested loops? Check itertools first.

cards.title: functools.lru_cache
cards.explanation: Slap `@lru_cache` on a pure function and Python automatically caches its results — repeat calls with the same args become instant. Perfect for recursive functions, expensive lookups, or memoizing API parsers.
cards.takeaway: @lru_cache: free memoization for pure functions.

cards.title: Mutable default arguments trap
cards.explanation: Writing `def f(items=[])` looks innocent but the list is created once and shared across every call — leading to ghost data leaking between invocations. Use `None` as the default and create the list inside the function.
cards.takeaway: Never use mutable defaults — use None instead.

cards.title: async and await
cards.explanation: `async def` defines a coroutine; `await` pauses it until something finishes — usually I/O like a network call. It lets one thread juggle thousands of slow operations at once, instead of blocking on each.
cards.takeaway: async/await: handle many slow I/O calls in one thread.

cards.title: Threads vs processes vs async
cards.explanation: Threads are good for I/O but limited by Python's GIL for CPU work. Multiprocessing sidesteps the GIL by spawning real processes. Async is the lightweight champion for huge numbers of I/O tasks. Pick by bottleneck, not by habit.
cards.takeaway: I/O-bound → async/threads. CPU-bound → processes.
